**Verdict: LEGAL.** The math clears with room to spare: Portland sends out $34,890,215 between Cam Amadi and Kellen Okoro, and because that outgoing figure sits above $29,974,000 you land in the 125% + $250,000 band, giving you a ceiling of $43,862,768. Goran Boateng's $43,183,713 slides in underneath it.

The part worth flagging is the aftermath. Taking back more than 100% of outgoing salary hard-caps you at the first apron of $178,132,000, and aggregating two salaries in a single deal hard-caps you at the second apron of $188,931,000 -- when two triggers fire, the tighter one governs, so you are locked at $178,132,000 for the balance of the league year.

Payroll lands at $146,333,520 on the apron sheet, which leaves $31,798,480 of headroom under that ceiling. Comfortable today, but understand what you have bought: for the rest of the season every signing, waiver claim and follow-up trade gets measured against $178,132,000 rather than against the tax line. You are also going from 13 players to 12 in this deal, so budget one of those roster spots and its salary before you treat that $31,798,480 as spendable.

You are $16,492,328 over the second apron, and the two tools you would normally reach for to fix that are already gone. Above the second apron, salaries cannot be combined in a trade and no cash may be sent -- so this gets solved with one contract going out the door, in a deal where nothing meaningful comes back.

Three names do it on their own. Rashad Rees at $18,340,478 is the minimum-viable version, clearing the line by $1,848,150. Amari Whitfield at $44,797,109 clears by $28,304,781. Nikola Whitfield at $57,736,350 clears by $41,244,022.

My read: the Rees version is the cheapest in basketball terms but leaves you managing the line to the dollar all season -- one in-season addition and you are back over, with the same restrictions and no aggregation to trade your way out. The two Whitfield contracts actually restore your ability to operate at the deadline. Whichever you choose, price in the sweetener. Because you cannot attach cash and cannot package a second salary to make the money work, the acquiring team either wants the contract or has to be paid in picks to absorb it, and that draft compensation is the real cost of getting under $16,492,328 of overage.

Not remotely. Memphis carries $165,010,219 in salaries plus likely incentives, and with nothing in unlikely incentives on this sheet the apron salary is the same $165,010,219. That is $22,884,781 below the $187,895,000 tax line, $30,934,781 below the first apron at $195,945,000, and $42,813,781 below the second apron at $207,824,000.

Practically, none of the apron machinery touches you. You can aggregate salaries in trades, send cash, shop the buyout market and use your exceptions without a second-apron veto hanging over any of it.

The constraint that actually binds here is roster count, not payroll. You are carrying 13, so two more contracts are coming before opening night, and those come out of the $22,884,781 before you spend a dollar on outside help. One thing to keep in front of you when you do spend it: using a mid-level or bi-annual exception installs a hard cap at an apron for the whole league year. At this payroll that ceiling is remote, but it is the sort of thing that gets forgotten in July and remembered in February.

**Verdict: LEGAL.** Luka Novak's $4,198,295 sits at or below the $9,096,000 threshold, which puts you in the most generous matching band there is -- 200% plus $250,000, permitting up to $8,646,590 back. Marcus Ferreira at $7,632,522 fits with real margin.

What the deal costs you is optionality. Taking back more than 100% of outgoing salary hard-caps Chicago at the first apron, $209,015,000, for the rest of the league year. Payroll after the trade is $169,560,134, so you would carry $39,454,866 of room beneath that ceiling -- no squeeze this season under any plausible scenario.

Still, a hard cap is a hard cap: it is absolute, it survives every subsequent transaction, and it removes your ability to go above the apron at the deadline even if the right opportunity presents itself. On a team sitting $39,454,866 clear that is an acceptable price. I would just make sure the front office notes it now, because the answer to a February question on apron flexibility changes the moment this trade is called in.

The bill is $121,097,010. Tax salary is $221,808,393 against a $187,895,000 line, so $33,913,393 is exposed, and the escalator does the rest.

Bracket by bracket, each $5,685,000 wide: the first $5,685,000 costs $5,685,000 at $1.00 per dollar; the second costs $7,106,250 at $1.25; the third jumps to $19,897,500 at $3.50; the fourth to $27,003,750 at $4.75; the fifth to $29,846,250 at $5.25; and the final $5,488,393 lands at $5.75 for $31,558,260.

Two things to sit with. First, look at where your marginal dollar lives -- at $5.75 per dollar, shedding a single mid-sized contract is worth several times its face value in tax relief, which is a very different calculus from trimming payroll on a team just over the line. Second, you forfeit the distribution: half the tax pool is paid out to non-taxpaying teams and you receive none of it. That is real money on top of the $121,097,010, and it is the part that usually gets left out of ownership presentations.

**Verdict: ILLEGAL.** The gap is $267,725, and as drawn it kills the deal. Washington's apron salary is $203,897,414, over the first apron, and an apron team's matching ceiling is exactly 100% of what it sends out -- so Nico Kalinic's $5,765,857 permits $5,765,857 back, and Jalil Jokubaitis at $6,033,582 is past it.

The fix is small and mechanical. Add at least $267,725 more of outgoing salary, which a single minimum contract alongside Kalinic accomplishes, or bring in a third team to absorb the difference. The basketball stays exactly as drawn.

The larger point is that this constraint governs the rest of your year, not just this trade. Even completed, you would sit at $204,165,139 in apron salary, still above the first apron, which means every deal from here has to bring back less than it sends. Build your deadline board on that assumption -- one-for-ones where you shed money -- rather than discovering it trade by trade.

Working strictly from the 2029-30 thresholds in front of me, since those are the only figures that govern this question: Atlanta's apron salary is $196,310,987. Against the first apron of $187,710,000 you are over. Against the second apron of $199,090,000 you are under, with $2,779,013 of clearance.

That distinction is the whole answer. As a first-apron team you lose the non-taxpayer mid-level and the bi-annual exception, you are held to 100% salary matching in trades, and you are shut out of the buyout market for anyone whose pre-waiver salary exceeded the non-taxpayer mid-level. What you keep -- the taxpayer mid-level, the ability to aggregate contracts, the ability to send cash -- all survives up to $199,090,000 and disappears the instant you cross it.

Worth saying plainly: run $196,310,987 against a threshold table from a different season and it reads as second-apron territory, and you would spend the year planning around bans that do not apply to you. Use the numbers for the season you are actually operating in. And protect the $2,779,013 -- it is thin enough that a single mid-sized in-season addition erases it, and using the taxpayer mid-level would hard-cap you at $199,090,000 anyway, which makes that line your practical ceiling either way.

**Verdict: LEGAL.** This one works because the money moves in the right direction: Marcus Kearns out at $27,426,695, Isaiah Nakamura in at $22,816,874, against a matching limit of $27,426,695. Indiana is over the first apron, so the ceiling is exactly 100% of outgoing salary and you are inside it with room. Because the return is smaller than the outgoing salary, the trade leaves you free of any hard cap.

The strategic picture is more interesting than the legality. Indiana starts at $226,326,335 and finishes at $221,716,514 -- still above the second apron. You shed a meaningful amount of salary and stay in exactly the same tier, which means the aggregation ban and the cash ban remain in force, and the mid-levels remain unavailable.

So if the real objective is escaping the second apron, this is progress that does not finish the job, and it makes the next step harder rather than easier: with aggregation off the table, whatever comes next has to come off a single contract, and you have just traded away one of the larger ones you could have used. If getting under that line is a genuine priority, I would want this deal restructured to send out more, or paired with a plan for a second single-salary dump that you have already sourced.

**Verdict: LEGAL.** Waiving and stretching Elijah Rees spreads $72,800,000 across five seasons -- twice the two years remaining, plus one -- for $14,560,000 of dead money per year. Your ceiling is 15% of the cap, which is $23,197,050 against the $154,647,000 figure, and you carry $0 in previously stretched money, so the entire $14,560,000 fits with $8,637,050 to spare.

Now the part worth saying out loud: legal and advisable are different questions. You are converting a two-year obligation into a five-year one, which parks $14,560,000 on your books in seasons four and five, when this roster will look nothing like today's, and it consumes most of the room under a ceiling you might want later for a mistake that has yet to happen.

The case for doing it is in-season relief -- $14,560,000 against the tax line is dramatically cheaper than the full freight, and if you are anywhere near a bracket that matters, the savings are immediate. The case against is that you are the team that has to sign free agents in 2029 with dead money on the sheet. If there is a live trade market for the contract, exhaust it first; the stretch is the right call only when the alternative is carrying the full number and you are confident the cap grows into $14,560,000.

Your toolkit this summer is short but flexible, and the reason is that you are a cap-space team rather than an over-the-cap team. Miami's apron salary is $155,316,639, comfortably under the tax line and under the cap itself, and that fork determines everything downstream: a team operating with room does not get the mid-level exceptions at all.

The sequence is therefore straightforward. Spend the room on your priority target. Once it is used, the room exception at $9,366,000 becomes your one remaining above-minimum tool, and it triggers no hard cap -- which is genuinely valuable, since every mid-level path would install one. Then fill out the roster with minimum contracts, which stay available at any payroll level and also trigger nothing. You are at 14 players, so you have at least one spot to account for.

The trade-off deserves an explicit decision rather than a default. Going the room route costs you the $15,044,000 non-taxpayer mid-level, the $6,064,000 taxpayer mid-level and the $5,477,000 bi-annual. If your usable room ends up smaller than $15,044,000 after accounting for cap holds, staying over the cap and using the full mid-level is the better instrument -- and that is a decision to make before you renounce anything, because it is effectively irreversible once you do.

**Verdict: LEGAL.** Over the first apron the salary-matching test is bare arithmetic -- 100% of outgoing salary, with none of the expansion that under-the-tax teams enjoy -- so Julian Beauchamp's $4,868,202 sets the ceiling at $4,868,202. Rashad Sabonis comes back at $3,584,836, well inside it, and because the return is smaller than what you send, the deal triggers no hard cap.

Two side effects belong in front of you. Apron salary drops from $184,826,541 to $183,543,175, which is a genuine saving in a season where every dollar above the tax line carries a multiple -- though your tier is unchanged, since you were over the first apron before and remain over it after.

The other is roster count. You go from 15 players to 14, and that spot will get filled eventually; at this payroll even a minimum contract is a taxed dollar. So treat $183,543,175 as a temporary number rather than a floor, and if the point of the exercise is banking the savings, leave the 15th spot open as long as the rotation allows.

Toronto's bill is $12,684,230 -- small as these things go, though the position matters more than the number. Tax salary is $211,788,184 against the $200,428,000 line, which puts $11,360,184 into the tax. The first $6,064,000 of that is charged at $1.00 per dollar for $6,064,000; the remaining $5,296,184 falls into the second bracket at $1.25 per dollar for $6,620,230.

Here is what I would brief ownership on. You have cleared the cheapest bracket and are well into the second, and the schedule escalates sharply from there -- the next bracket costs several times what the first one did. Payroll added between now and the deadline gets priced at the margin, so an in-season addition costs considerably more than its face value suggests.

Clearing the $11,360,184 entirely does two things, and teams routinely account for only one. It erases the $12,684,230, and it restores your share of the tax distribution -- taxpaying teams receive none of the 50% paid out to non-taxpayers. If you are within one salary dump of the line, the total swing is materially larger than the bill you are looking at.

**Verdict: ILLEGAL.** The blocker is roster size, not money. San Antonio already carries 15 players, and the 15-man limit has to be cleared before any signing gets processed, whatever exception you are using.

On the money side, everything works -- which is why this is worth revisiting once the roster is right. Malik Okoro at $4,678,503 fits inside the $6,064,000 taxpayer mid-level with $1,385,497 of the exception unspent. Apron salary would move from $212,498,301 to $217,176,804, and the second-apron hard cap the taxpayer MLE installs -- $221,686,000 -- would still leave $4,509,196 of room.

Two cautions before you go clear a spot. Waiving a player removes him from the roster but leaves his salary on your books, so a waiver buys you the roster space without buying you any room; if you need both, the spot has to come out of a trade that sends salary away. And the hard cap attaches the instant you spend a dollar of the taxpayer mid-level, so you would be committing to operate inside $4,509,196 for the remainder of the league year in exchange for a $4,678,503 player. That is the real price, and it is worth more scrutiny than the salary is.

One real exception, plus minimums. Utah's apron salary is $180,778,389, above the first apron of $178,132,000, and that single fact removes the non-taxpayer mid-level and the bi-annual exception outright -- neither is available to a team over that line. The room exception goes too; it belongs to teams operating under the cap, which this roster emphatically is not.

What survives is the taxpayer mid-level at $5,168,000 and minimum contracts, which stay available at any payroll and trigger nothing. Also intact, and worth remembering because they are the tools most teams actually use in-season: you can still aggregate salaries in a trade and still send cash, since those bans arrive at the second apron, $188,931,000, rather than the first.

The string attached to the taxpayer MLE is the one to think hard on. Spend a dollar of it and you are hard-capped at $188,931,000 for the whole league year, and you are starting from $180,778,389 with a full 15-man roster. In-season churn alone eats into that. I would want certainty that the full $5,168,000 is going to a rotation player before accepting a ceiling that tight -- otherwise minimums keep you flexible and cost you almost nothing in practice.

**Verdict: ILLEGAL.** The salary matching misses by $16,503,166. Utah sends out $55,878,085 combining Darnell Osei at $8,840,514 and Andre Petrov at $47,037,571, which is above the $32,971,000 threshold and therefore in the 125% + $250,000 band, allowing a maximum return of $70,097,606. Corey Reddish at $86,600,772 is far beyond that.

This is a structural gap, not a rounding problem -- you need a third team with room to absorb the difference, or substantially more salary heading out.

Worth seeing what the deal would have done even with the money solved. Aggregating two salaries hard-caps you at the second apron, $207,824,000; taking back more than 100% hard-caps you at the first apron, $195,945,000; the tighter one governs. You would have landed at $174,054,720, leaving $21,890,280 under that first-apron ceiling. Comfortable on paper, but you would be a team that just absorbed an $86,600,772 contract with a permanent ceiling attached, and you are at 15 players already. If Reddish is genuinely the target, I would build it as a three-team deal from the start rather than trying to patch the two-team version.

**Verdict: ILLEGAL.** Two separate failures, either one fatal on its own. Matching first: Portland is over the first apron at $206,505,095, so the ceiling on the return is 100% of the $24,744,788 you send out -- exactly $24,744,788 -- and Elijah Reddish at $28,176,969 exceeds it by $3,432,181. Then the hard cap: combining Goran Reddish at $3,291,481 and Santi Beauchamp at $21,453,307 in one deal hard-caps you at the second apron, $207,824,000, and the post-trade payroll of $209,937,276 sits $2,113,276 above that line.

The second failure is the instructive one. Even if you found the extra outgoing salary to satisfy the matching test, the aggregation trigger fires the moment you combine two contracts, and the hard cap it installs is a wall you would already be standing behind on the day of the trade. Aggregation is effectively unavailable to you at this payroll regardless of what the rulebook technically permits.

So the shape that works is one contract out, less money coming back, or a third team taking Reddish's salary and routing you someone smaller. Beauchamp alone for a player under $21,453,307 is the version I would explore first.

**Verdict: ILLEGAL.** Stretching a one-year, $80,200,000 obligation spreads it across three seasons at $26,733,333 a year, and that figure alone exceeds the ceiling before anything else is counted. You are already carrying $12,100,000 of previously stretched dead money, so the total becomes $38,833,333 against a limit of $21,088,200 -- 15% of the $140,588,000 cap. That is $17,745,133 over the line in each of three seasons.

For the waiver to work as drawn, Luka Brantley would have to give back $53,235,399, which is $17,745,133 across three seasons. No agent entertains that on an $80,200,000 guarantee, so treat this path as closed.

The realistic options are the ones nobody likes. Waive without stretching and carry $80,200,000 on this season's books. Keep him and trade the contract, paying whatever the market demands to move it. Or wait until the existing $12,100,000 of stretched money rolls off and revisit the arithmetic then. I would model the straight waiver first -- it is brutal in one season, but it leaves the out-years clean, and the version that puts $26,733,333 on your sheet through the end of the decade is how teams end up rebuilding with one hand tied.

**Verdict: ILLEGAL.** Miami's apron salary is $215,312,439, over the first apron, and that status alone decides it: apron teams match at 100%, so Micah Ibarra's $25,084,794 going out permits exactly $25,084,794 coming back. Dante Rees at $30,684,404 misses by $5,599,610.

There is a second reason to pause even after you solve the matching. The deal would put you at $220,912,049 in apron salary -- $5,599,610 of net new money on a payroll that is already an apron payroll -- and that pushes you right up against the second apron, where the aggregation ban and the cash ban take hold and where the tax rate on marginal dollars becomes punishing. You would be paying a premium for the privilege of losing flexibility.

If Rees is the player you want, the structures are a third team that takes Ibarra and sends you nothing, or a package with a second outgoing contract. Be careful with the second: aggregating triggers a second-apron hard cap, and at $220,912,049 you would be accepting a ceiling you are practically touching. My honest read is that this trade wants to be smaller than it is.

**Verdict: LEGAL.** Jalil Kearns out at $11,930,035, Julian Rees in at $10,232,165, against a ceiling of $11,930,035 -- Indiana is above the first apron, so matching is dollar-for-dollar with no expansion, and you are inside it. Sending out more than you take back keeps the deal clear of any hard cap.

The context deserves bluntness, though. Indiana starts at $225,274,914 and finishes at $223,577,044, which is still above the second apron. You save money and stay in precisely the same tier, so the aggregation ban and the cash ban remain in force and the mid-levels remain out of reach.

If escaping the second apron is the actual objective, this is a step that falls short of it, and it makes the next step harder: with aggregation unavailable, whatever comes next has to come off a single contract, and you have just moved one of the mid-sized salaries you could have used. Either enlarge this deal so it clears the second apron on its own, or line up the second single-salary move before you call this one in.

**Verdict: LEGAL.** Detroit ships $10,079,630 in Kristaps Cordero and brings back $7,676,236 for Darnell Amadi, comfortably inside the $10,079,630 ceiling that 100% matching imposes on a team over the first apron. Because the return is smaller than the outgoing salary, the trade triggers no hard cap and leaves your flexibility exactly where it was.

The value is in the payroll movement: $213,075,717 down to $210,672,323, and every dollar of that reduction is coming off a payroll sitting above the second apron, where the tax rates are at their steepest. That alone justifies the deal if the basketball is a wash.

Where it falls short is tier. You are above the second apron before and after, so the aggregation ban, the cash ban and the loss of the mid-levels all stay in place, and $210,672,323 is still a long way from relief. Treat this as tax mitigation rather than a path back under, and if the goal is genuinely to get under that line, you need moves an order of magnitude larger than this one.

**Verdict: ILLEGAL.** Two independent blockers, and the first is structural. The bi-annual exception is unavailable to any team over the first apron, and Sacramento's apron salary before this signing is $206,764,839 -- well past that line. The exception simply does not exist for you this season, so the size of the contract is beside the point.

Second, the roster is full at 15. Even an exception you did have would require clearing a spot before it could be used.

Before you reach for the obvious substitute, run the numbers on it: using the taxpayer mid-level installs a hard cap at the second apron, and adding $4,325,013 puts you at $211,089,852. That route breaks the hard cap on day one, so it fails as well. What is left for Devonte Sabonis is a minimum contract, which stays available at any payroll and triggers nothing -- and even that requires a roster spot first. Given where $211,089,852 sits on the tax schedule, I would want the basketball case to be overwhelming before you clear a spot to make any of this happen.

Good news first: the gap is $1,195,296. Atlanta's apron salary is $209,019,296 against a second apron of $207,824,000, which by the standards of these problems is a rounding error -- one modest contract out the door solves it.

The constraint is that it has to be one contract. Above the second apron you cannot aggregate salaries in a trade and you cannot include cash, so the fix is a single-salary move with nothing meaningful coming back. Four names on this sheet do it alone: Trey Reddish at $2,703,892 clears by $1,508,596, Micah Dumont at $2,963,869 clears by $1,768,573, Bogdan Nakamura at $4,115,970 clears by $2,920,674, and Alperen Reddish at $6,527,478 clears by $5,332,182.

My advice is to go past the minimum viable version. Reddish or Dumont technically gets you under, but $1,508,596 or $1,768,573 of cushion evaporates the first time you sign anyone in-season, and you would spend the year managing the line to the dollar. Nakamura or Alperen Reddish gives you enough margin to actually operate at the deadline. One useful side effect either way: you are at 15 players, so moving a contract out creates the roster spot you will want for a minimum signing later, which is the cheapest way to backfill.

The number that matters is $154,693,794, and the reason it differs from $148,593,794 is the incentive structure on three contracts. Salaries plus likely incentives come to $148,593,794; the $6,100,000 of unlikely incentives carried by Trey Whitfield, Nikola Petrov and Deni Novak counts toward apron salary only -- never toward cap or tax salary -- and that is exactly the distinction that catches teams out at the deadline.

At $154,693,794 you are $45,734,206 below the tax line, $54,321,206 below the first apron and $66,992,206 below the second. No apron restriction touches you: aggregate salaries in trades, send cash, shop the buyout market, all of it is open.

The offseason opportunity here is that you can be the third team. Clubs pinned above the aprons need someone to absorb salary and route contracts, and they pay in picks for the service -- you are one of the few franchises positioned to sell that. Just make sure your trade desk is measuring against the apron figure rather than the tax figure when they do it. The $6,100,000 gap between $148,593,794 and $154,693,794 rides along on every calculation, and that is the sort of discrepancy that turns a signed-off deal into a rejected one.

Minimum contracts. That is the whole list.

Orlando's apron salary is $214,101,075, which puts you above the second apron of $207,824,000, and at that altitude the exception menu collapses entirely. The non-taxpayer mid-level and the bi-annual are gone the moment you pass the first apron at $195,945,000. The taxpayer mid-level -- the lifeline that over-the-tax teams normally live on -- disappears above the second apron, so you have no mid-level of any kind. The room exception requires operating under the cap, which is a different universe from where this roster sits. Minimum deals remain available at every payroll level and trigger no hard cap.

So free agency is a scouting exercise rather than a spending one. You are competing for veterans who will take the minimum for a role, and you are leaning on your own draft picks and two-way contracts for depth. The operational point: you are carrying 13 players, which means multiple spots to fill with a single instrument. Start those conversations early -- the good minimum-salary veterans sign quickly, and the buyout names you might otherwise chase are largely off-limits to a team in your position anyway.

**Verdict: ILLEGAL.** Every piece of the cap math works and the signing still fails, because Charlotte is carrying 15 players and the roster limit sits in front of every exception. Clear a spot and this becomes a live question again.

For the record on the money: Elijah Osei at $4,462,628 fits inside the $5,685,000 taxpayer mid-level with $1,222,372 unspent, apron salary moves from $181,797,866 to $186,260,494, and the second-apron hard cap the exception installs -- $207,824,000 -- leaves $21,563,506 of room. The payroll side is nowhere near binding.

Here is the part I would push back on. At $181,797,866 you are under the tax line, which means the full non-taxpayer mid-level should be available to you, and it is considerably larger than the taxpayer version. Spending the smaller exception on a $4,462,628 player when the bigger one is sitting there is leaving value on the table. The trade-off is the hard cap -- the non-taxpayer route caps you at the first apron rather than the second, a tighter ceiling but still far above where you sit. Clear the roster spot first, then decide which exception you are actually spending; the answer is probably the bigger one.

**Verdict: ILLEGAL.** This one fails before the money even comes up. Washington's apron salary is $209,607,080, above the second apron of $188,931,000, and a second-apron team may not combine two salaries in a single trade -- pairing Micah Rees at $5,760,255 with Jaylen Ibarra at $10,932,579 is prohibited on its face, whatever comes back the other way.

The matching test fails too, for completeness. $16,692,834 out, 100% matching because you are over the first apron, so $16,692,834 is the ceiling, and Micah Ferreira at $17,668,846 clears it by $976,012.

The aggregation ban is what should shape your entire deadline. Every deal is one contract at a time, and every deal has to bring back less than it sends. If Ferreira is the target, the workable version is Ibarra alone for a player under $10,932,579, or a third team that absorbs Ferreira's salary and routes you someone smaller. And note where this trade would have left you -- $210,583,092 -- which is not a payroll one clever transaction fixes. If ownership wants out of the second apron, that conversation needs to start with which large contract is leaving, not with which package to assemble.

You are $14,882,251 above the second apron, and that number governs everything you do this year. Utah's salaries plus likely incentives come to $229,968,251, but $6,600,000 of unlikely incentives on Rashad Rees, Kobe Amadi and Devonte Brantley counts toward apron salary -- so the operative figure is $236,568,251, not the $229,968,251 a tax sheet would show you. Measured against the thresholds, that is $36,140,251 above the tax line, $27,553,251 above the first apron and $14,882,251 above the second.

What that means in practice: no aggregating salaries in trades, no cash in deals, no mid-level of any kind, no buyout-market signings above the mid-level, and minimum contracts as your only route to add a player. Stay here through the end of the season and the frozen first-round pick provision comes into play as well, which is the restriction with the longest tail.

One lever people miss. That $6,600,000 of unlikely incentives is apron salary you are carrying for money that may never be earned. If any of those three contracts is movable, you clear more apron salary than the base figure implies -- it is the cheapest yard available on this sheet. Beyond that, closing a $14,882,251 gap with only 13 players on the roster means a single significant contract has to go out, unaggregated, with nothing coming back.

$223,271,999. That is New Orleans's apron salary measured against the thresholds you pasted, and it makes you a first-apron team rather than a second-apron one -- the first apron you have given me is $219,429,000 and the second is $232,731,000, so you sit between them with $9,459,001 of clearance.

That distinction drives the entire plan.
